sections.title: Employment Contract
sections.text:
I am Clementia, an Aegirian. It is a pleasure to meet you.

Depending on context, "I'm glad" can mean the whole range of important implications of sea-land cooperation, or it can really just mean "I'm glad."

sections.title: Token
sections.text: A finger sheath bearing Clementia's fingerprint. A token belonging to her alone, and of course, the key to all her authority in Aegir. You know you must keep it with the utmost care.

sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Clementia, Aegir's Honorary Legion Commander, Honorary Consul, and Honorary Chief War Architect, is responsible for all projects Aegir has carried out or plans to carry out on land. She currently assists Rhodes Island's work in Iberia and Aegir as a partner, and hopes to establish cooperative relations with more political entities on land through Rhodes Island.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests reveal clear, normal outlines of internal organs, and no abnormal shadows have been detected. Originium granules have not been detected in the circulatory system and there is no sign of infection. At this time, this operator is believed to be uninfected.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 0%
Operator Clementia shows no signs of Originium infection.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.009u/L
Operator Clementia rarely comes into contact with Originium.

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
[A trial-use feedback report, from Clementia to the Weapons Design Institute]
Thank you for your hard work. Miniaturizing a ship-mounted cutting tool to this degree must have been quite an arduous task.
Judging from this round of trial use, there are no longer many issues in terms of functionality or ease of use. The previously discovered problem—the blade's high-frequency vibration fracturing the user's wrist bones—has not recurred (the fracture has healed as well; thank you for your care last time).
When cutting most inorganic materials, its performance is very stable. But against Seaborn tissue, the Grade IV weapons technology mounted on the sword fails to take effect reliably, and some tissue slowly regenerates even after being cut.
I hope it can be improved.
Besides that, I'd like to ask a favor of you: please engrave a line on the blade for me.
Please engrave this line:
"You are the salt of the earth."

[An etymological study, written by Clementia at the Language Design Institute]
"You are the salt of the earth." A phrase of praise originating in Iberia. Like most of the Liberi living in Iberia today, the phrase originally came from Laterano; "You are the sugar of the earth" was its original form.
"You are the sugar of the earth"—so exclaimed Laterano's first saint from the heart, upon first growing sugar crops in the earth. The phrase was recorded in "The Travels of the Saints" and passed down through generations in Laterano. Considering how the Laterans love sweets more than life itself, it's not hard to understand why the phrase carries a sense of praise.
After reaching Iberia, the phrase quickly changed. In the years when Iberia's salt industry flourished and Iberian palates were gradually tamed by the sea, the "sugar" in the phrase naturally evolved into "salt." The taste and economic value of salt together gave the phrase a strongly laudatory meaning, and as the salt trade prospered, the phrase spread to the various nations in the south of the continent.
"You are the salt of the earth," the land-dwellers say in praise of all manner of good things.

[A conversation record, Clementia and a researcher at the Weapons Design Institute]
"Consul Clementia, I don't quite understand. If it's a phrase of praise from the land-dwellers, shouldn't it be engraved on a gift for them? Why engrave it on a sword?"
"To remind myself."
"Remind... of what?"
"If I told you that on land, salt is the most important seasoning, would you find that strange?"
"Season things with salt? How is that any different from not seasoning them at all?"
"Just because we live in one enormous pot of saltwater soup doesn't mean we can assume everyone thinks as little of salt as we do. At the very least, I should remember that... especially on occasions when the sword must be drawn."

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
When I arrived at the dressing room, Consul Clementia was already sitting in front of the mirror. The hair on her right side wasn't pinned up as usual, and the curtain of hair hanging down just covered her eyes. I'd guess she couldn't see herself in the mirror like that.
I asked her how she'd like it done, and after thinking for a moment, she asked me: "What should a human look like?"
I froze.
Then she looked up, smiled, and told me it was a joke, and to just do it the way I usually do.
—A makeup artist at the Public Activities Administration

Consuls don't always need to appear in public; rather, most of the time only a few of them do. Miliarium's Science Consul has never given any speech in public; all of his views are conveyed on his behalf by Technology Consul Clementia.
In fact, Clementia's public appearances go far beyond Miliarium. Nationwide grand councils, technology exchange exhibitions held for all cities, and the academic development sync programs every citizen watches are often hosted by Clementia. Today, the one who must represent Aegir in establishing relations with the nations of the land is also Clementia.
Of course, there have been proposals to have lifelike avatars and synthetic voices handle this work, but such proposals are only ever overwhelmingly voted down. A civilization that invented simulated personalities with autonomous thought over two hundred years ago, yet still installs simple logic modules capable only of passive response in all kinds of machinery, can only mean one thing: it places too much weight on the irreplaceability of humans.
When Clementia was first assessed as fit to serve as Consul, the Development Planning Institute took her image into consideration. Aegir needed someone to speak on its behalf, and that person needed to appear kind, friendly, composed, and rational.
Most importantly, she needed to look like an ideal "human," an image the public could naturally identify with out of nothing more than their pride in having been born human.
They judged that Clementia's appearance, bearing, and manner of speech all met the requirements. At least, that was the conclusion reached by several humanities research institutes after lengthy, systematic fieldwork.
She was probably bewildered, being told without any warning that she was the ideal image of a "human."
—A liaison at the Public Activities Administration

So whenever Clementia has free time, she goes to be a "model." Not for the painters at the Visual Arts Creation Institute, of course, but here at our Paleontological Research Institute.
We survey her head fins, tail, and skeletal structure, and she cooperates by performing all kinds of movements so we can record her motion patterns.
Combining her complete genome sequence provided by the Genetic Science Research Institute with literature provided by the Prehistory Research Institute, we were able to reconstruct fairly thoroughly the ancient species to which Clementia once belonged (which the prehistoric civilization called the "giant oceanic manta ray"). Thanks to the large amount of research material Clementia enthusiastically provided (mainly from herself), we were even able to build complete skeletal and muscular models of the species and simulate its movement on a computer.
I don't know why Clementia is so keen on this, but most of the time I'd venture to say she just looks like she's...
Simply enjoying the fact that she is a manta ray.
—A researcher at the Paleontological Research Institute

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
[A letter of complaint, from Clementia's physician]
You almost never see Clementia sleep.
Don't tell me Aegirians don't need to follow the cycle of sunset and moonrise. I'm Aegirian too. Freely deciding your schedule presupposes that it includes at least some "rest."
Why Clementia doesn't sleep, I don't care; she always has a reason. If it's not her duties as Consul, it's excuses like "the data hub's login time seems half a second slow" or "the airlock drainage sounds a little different than usual"—in short, she's uneasy about this and can't let go of that. Every time she goes to see the relevant person in charge about such things, she's gone for seven or eight hours. After that, she goes straight to the Consul's meditation chamber to continue her actual work.
As you can imagine, Clementia's health is not very promising. Even if I didn't remind her often enough, Consul Heratia specially assigned her a custom Little Helper to remind her of it at all times. But most of the time, she kept this Little Helper's health monitoring module switched off.
And that's not even the worst of it.
The worst of it is when she occasionally does decide to sleep. Only then does she turn on the Little Helper's health monitoring module. The Little Helper faithfully reports her less-than-promising physical condition: her bundle branch block, the nodules in her fin tissue... Consul Heratia says that at some point, this became the only way Clementia could fall asleep: listening to these reports.
I don't understand. How can a person feel... reassured by the deterioration of their own health? It's practically a provocation against medicine.

[A research record, from the Intelligent Machinery Design Institute]
The moment the Legion fleet returned to port, a malfunctioning Little Helper was sent to my lab. Even as the logistics module unloaded it, it was still faithfully broadcasting the information it had gathered on the battlefield in a clear, bright voice:
"Agrippa, deceased. Cause of death: thoracic crush caused by ship engine explosion.
"Flaminia, deceased. Cause of death: nitrogen narcosis caused by damage to deep-dive armor.
"Paulinus, deceased. Cause of death: acute aberration caused by Seaborn cell invasion."
Before the support fleet found the wreckage of that engineering mothership, it had spent seven days surrounded by a swarm of Seaborn. The only things salvaged from it were one survivor and this malfunctioning Little Helper. The Little Helper's logic components were severely damaged; it didn't follow commands, couldn't be operated, and couldn't even be shut down. Short of smashing its voice unit with a hammer, I couldn't think of any way to make it quiet. It just kept repeating every crew member's information, over, and over, and over again: not only the deaths of hundreds of colleagues and how each of them died, but also the survivor's injuries, and... how many days she had left to live. Pulling the data revealed that it had repeated its report one hundred and fifty-three times over those seven days. It doesn't take any expert knowledge of psychology to imagine how tormenting it must have been, in such a cramped, sealed space, with only corpses that no longer resembled people for company, to listen for hundreds of hours straight to these broadcasts pronouncing death.
When I visited that survivor, I asked her why she hadn't destroyed this Little Helper's voice unit, since she clearly had a sword in hand.
She couldn't speak yet at the time, so she just wrote these words for me: "I've never seen a Little Helper malfunction like that. Don't you want to study it?"
I later heard that she had guarded that cabin for seven whole days in order to preserve a precious tissue sample of a "Primal." They awarded her an honorary title and made her Legion Commander... but I find it hard to imagine how she could see that as any kind of honor.

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
People like us, who spend years moving around Aegir, can easily tell which cities Clementia has had a hand in.
If you walk into your room and find a small metal bottle on the desk, that's Clementia's handiwork. The compressed gas inside was collected from your previous residence; if you're willing to open it, your new home will smell exactly like the old one.
But when I stayed in Miliarium for a while, what she prepared for me was a scented candle. Just an ordinary scent, completely unrelated to where I'd been staying before. She probably knew the Abyssal Hunters' research institute always had a lingering smell of Seaborn, and she knew I didn't like that smell.
Oh, she even knew I liked candles.
I don't know why she goes to such trouble, but I'd guess it's probably to give her city a bit more of a feeling of "home."
If someone applied to move to her city for those reasons, I wouldn't be surprised. At least, if I weren't an Abyssal Hunter, I certainly would have.
—Laurentina, Abyssal Hunters

Everyone knew what it meant for us to apply to move to Miliarium at a time like this.
Everyone has an innate urge to destroy. The first time a child squashes a worm to death, they must feel happy. But the second time, the third, the fourth? What if all they could ever do in their whole life was keep coming up with one way, then another, then yet another, to kill worms?
This is what our lives are like. Trapped in an endless war, using all our creativity to design ways for the Seaborn to die, until our mouths and noses are clogged with the stench of Seaborn flesh. Then we bring our own children into the lab and have them carry on doing the same thing.
Some can accept it, but... not everyone. Not everyone. Rather than designing deaths for the Seaborn, I only want to be able to decide my own.
The Seaway Project was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. We all knew Miliarium would never return. A city, two understrength legions, from the homeland to the coastline... at least people would see it as a glorious sacrifice.
Quite a few people thought the same as I did. We spread out the times and places we submitted our applications as much as possible, and made up plenty of different versions of our reasons. As long as the Development Planning Institute couldn't see our intention to die, they would have no reason to reject our applications to move to Miliarium.
……
Thank goodness, they approved it.
—Avitus, citizen of Miliarium

The Development Planning Institute couldn't possibly approve any of their applications. We rejected them on grounds of insufficient qualifications, thinking that would be the end of it with no further complications.
Consul Heratia instructed that any news concerning this matter be kept strictly confidential from Consul Clementia... It's not hard to understand why. She has run Miliarium for so many years; if she found out those people came to her city only to die... at least, in Consul Heratia's words, this would be "detrimental to her maintaining a sound mental state befitting mission requirements."
But in the end, the one who intervened was none other than Consul Clementia. She bypassed our approval process and, citing mission requirements, moved those people into Miliarium through a special requisition channel.
...She knows. She has always known. She simply accepted it.
—An assessor at the Development Planning Institute

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
The Development Planning Institute's assessment report had already warned us in rather worried terms that everything Clementia had done since becoming Consul showed a strong sense of purpose. To quote the report directly, she seems to have "completely stopped doing anything simply for the sake of her own life."
This situation has not eased at all since she came ashore. We sometimes notice her leafing through Columbian comics with great interest, or carrying binoculars to observe fowlbeasts in the wilds of Rim Billiton. Of course, we always also find corresponding meetings on her schedule: with representatives of the Columbian government, or the heads of the Rim Billiton Mining Union.
In fact, when we finally arranged a talk with her about her work stress, what she discussed with our HR Operator was that Operator's favorite thing: uh, semi-fictional novels with historical themes.
After an hour of conversation, that Operator walked out of the meeting room and assured us we needn't worry about Clementia at all. But from the smile she couldn't suppress, we could tell she was just happy to have found someone who shared her hobby, which rarely happens. But how are we to know whether Clementia truly enjoys that, or whether her condition is so serious that she would make completely unnecessary preparations even for a simple conversation like this?
The supervisor later went to see her alone once more. Noticing how quickly the supervisor sidestepped the topics she raised, Clementia stopped avoiding the issue too.
"All of those things, reading comics, watching fowlbeasts, reading semi-fictional historical novels... do you really enjoy doing them?"
"I'm glad I had the chance to experience them. They were all truly interesting."
"Then what do you yourself truly want to do?"
"Does doing nothing count? Just floating on the surface of some water somewhere. Swimming's too much trouble, so I just float."
